h: From the headland down to the bays
p: Allow a good couple of hours for the castle itself, more if the weather's fine and you want to linger over the views. Once you're done, the walk back down is where the rest of your Scarborough day begins.

On the way, stop at St Mary's Church, just below the castle. In its churchyard is the grave of Anne Brontë, who died in Scarborough in 1849. It's a quiet, moving spot, and lots of literary fans make the pilgrimage.

From there, pick your bay. The South Bay is the classic seaside front, with the harbour, the lighthouse, fishing boats, chippies and the bright lights of the amusement arcades along Foreshore Road. It's loud, cheerful and everything a British seaside day should be, and a great place for a stroll with an ice cream. Some of the arcades along here have adult gaming areas that are strictly for over-18s, so keep the little ones to the family sections.

The North Bay is a touch calmer, with a sweeping beach, beach huts and Peasholm Park, a gorgeous Japanese-style park with a lake and pagoda. In summer, Peasholm is famous for its miniature naval battle re-enactments on the water, which are a real one-off. The North Bay Railway, a little miniature line, chugs along nearby too.

Culture fans should look for the Rotunda Museum, one of the earliest purpose-built museums in the country, and Scarborough Art Gallery. On a wet day, the Sea Life centre at the North Bay keeps kids happy. All in all, the castle is the perfect opening act for a full day by the sea.
